groups.title: L1 · Counting and basics
groups.desc: Equally likely outcomes, complements, inclusion–exclusion, ordered vs unordered counts.

groups.title: L2 · Conditioning and Bayes
groups.desc: Shrink the world, test independence with numbers, reverse a conditional.

groups.title: L3 · Expectation and variance
groups.desc: Weighted averages, linearity, how shifting and scaling change variance.

items.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is P(the sum is 7)?

opts.why: Six of the 36 equally likely ordered pairs sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), …, (6,1).
Treats the 11 possible sums as equally likely. They are not: 7 can happen six ways, 2 only one way.
Uses the target sum as the number of favorable outcomes. Count the pairs instead: there are 6.
That is P(sum = 4): three pairs out of 36.

items.why: List the 36 ordered pairs and count the ones that add to 7.

items.stem: When two fair dice are rolled, the 11 possible sums (2 through 12) are equally likely.

opts.why: The mix-up: the 36 ordered pairs are equally likely, so it is tempting to think the sums are too.
Corrected: the 36 ordered pairs are equally likely; the sums are not (7 has six pairs, 2 has one).

items.stem: A fair die is rolled 4 times. What is P(at least one six)? Give 3 decimals or an expression.
items.why: “At least one” is the complement of “none”. P(no six in 4 rolls) = (5/6)<sup>4</sup> = 625/1296.

items.stem: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is P(A ∪ B)?

opts.why: 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2: add both, subtract the overlap once.
Adds the two without subtracting the overlap, so the 0.2 in both is counted twice.
That is the intersection, the part in both.
That is P(A) alone; the union is at least as big as each event.

items.why: Inclusion–exclusion: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

items.stem: Which statements hold for any events A and B?

opts.why: Always: A and its complement split the sample space.
Always: the sum counts the overlap twice, so it can only be bigger.
Only when A and B are independent.
Always: the intersection is part of A.
Only when A and B are disjoint.

items.why: The two false ones need an extra condition: independence for the product, disjointness for the plain sum.

items.stem: A club of 8 people picks a president, a vice-president and a treasurer, all different people. How many ways?

opts.why: 8 choices for president, then 7, then 6: order matters because the titles differ.
That is C(8, 3), the number of 3-person groups. It ignores who holds which title.
8 · 8 · 8 lets one person hold two titles.
That is 4!, which does not match any step here.

items.stem: From 8 people, there are exactly 6 times as many (president, VP, treasurer) lists as there are 3-person committees.

opts.why: 336 / 56 = 6 = 3!: each committee can hand out its three titles in 3! ways.
The mix-up: thinking the two counts are equal, or differ by a factor of 3 instead of 3! = 6.

items.stem: Write inclusion–exclusion for three events A, B, C.
items.answer: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) − P(A ∩ B) − P(A ∩ C) − P(B ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C). Add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple back.

items.stem: One fair die is rolled. What is P(6 | the roll is even)?

opts.why: Given even, the world is {2, 4, 6}, and one of the three is a 6.
That ignores the information that the roll is even.
That is P(even), the condition itself.
That is P(not 6 | even).

items.stem: P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, then A and B are independent.

opts.why: The mix-up: “they have nothing in common” sounds like “they do not affect each other”.
Corrected: disjoint events with positive probability are dependent. Knowing A happened makes B impossible, so P(B | A) = 0 ≠ P(B).

items.stem: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects 90% of cases and gives a false positive for 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Which is closest to P(disease | positive)?

opts.why: Per 1000 people: 9 true positives and about 50 false positives, so 9/59 ≈ 15%.
That is P(positive | disease), how good the test is, not what a positive means.
90% − 5% does not correspond to any probability here.
That is the prior; it ignores the positive result.

items.why: Bayes: 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0495) ≈ 0.154. The rare disease keeps the posterior low.

items.stem: A fair coin is flipped twice. Which pairs of events are independent?

opts.t: “first flip is H” and “second flip is H”
opts.why: Independent: separate flips. 1/4 = 1/2 · 1/2.

opts.t: “first flip is H” and “both flips are H”
opts.why: Dependent: P(both | first H) = 1/2, but P(both) = 1/4.

opts.t: “first flip is H” and “the two flips match”
opts.why: Independent: P(match) = 1/2 and P(match | first H) = P(second H) = 1/2.

opts.t: “at least one H” and “both are T”
opts.why: Dependent: they are disjoint, so one rules out the other.

items.why: Check P(B | A) = P(B) with numbers; intuition about “sharing a flip” is unreliable.

items.stem: Factory A makes 60% of the parts and 2% of its parts are defective; factory B makes 40% and 5% of its parts are defective. What is P(a random part is defective)?

opts.why: The plain average of 2% and 5% ignores that factory A makes more parts.
2% + 5% adds rates from different groups without weights.
That is factory B’s share of defects, 0.4 · 0.05, only one branch.

items.why: Law of total probability: weight each factory’s defect rate by its share of production.

items.stem: If P(A) = P(B) > 0, then P(A | B) = P(B | A).

opts.why: Bayes: P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B), and the ratio is 1 when P(A) = P(B).
The mix-up: remembering that the two conditionals usually differ and forgetting when they agree.

items.stem: Same factories as above (A: 60% of parts, 2% defective; B: 40%, 5% defective). A part is defective. What is P(it came from B)?
items.why: Share of the defective branch that comes from B: 0.020 out of 0.032.

items.stem: X is the roll of a fair six-sided die. What is E[X]?

opts.why: Rounds the answer to a possible roll; E[X] need not be a value X takes.
The sum of the faces, not weighted by 1/6.
The largest value, not the average.

items.stem: The expected value of a random variable is always one of the values it can take.

opts.why: The mix-up: reading “expected” as “most likely”.
Corrected: E[X] is a weighted average. A fair die has E[X] = 3.5, which no roll shows.

items.stem: X takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is E[X]?
items.why: Multiply each value by its probability and add.

items.stem: Four people get their hats back in a random order. What is the expected number of people who get their own hat?

opts.why: Each person matches with probability 1/4; by linearity, 4 · 1/4 = 1.
That is one person’s chance, not the expected count.
That would mean everyone always matches.
That is P(everyone matches) = 1/4!.

items.why: Write the count as a sum of 4 indicators. Linearity works even though the indicators are dependent.

items.stem: Which hold for any random variables X, Y and constants a, b?

opts.why: Always: linearity needs no independence.
Always: linearity again.
Always: the shift b does not change spread, and scaling squares.
Needs X and Y uncorrelated (independence is enough). In general add 2 Cov(X, Y).
Needs independence (or zero covariance).
Always: it is an average of squares.

items.why: Expectation is linear without conditions; variance of a sum and expectation of a product need independence.

items.stem: X ~ Binomial(n = 20, p = 0.3). What is Var(X)?
items.why: A binomial is a sum of n independent Bernoulli(p), each with variance p(1 − p).

items.stem: Var(X) = 4. What is Var(3X − 2)?

opts.why: 3<sup>2</sup> · 4; the −2 shifts X but does not change its spread.
Multiplies by 3 instead of 3<sup>2</sup>.
3 · 4 − 2: applies the linear map to the variance itself.
9 · 4 − 2: the shift does not belong in the variance.

items.stem: For a Bernoulli(p) variable, the variance is largest when p = 0.5.

opts.why: p(1 − p) is a parabola with its peak 0.25 at p = 0.5.
The mix-up: thinking variance grows with p. At p = 1 the variable is constant and the variance is 0.
